title: SE201 Lesson 3: Decompose the system into a graph

scenes.text: Software engineering two oh one. Lesson three. [pause] Decompose the system into a graph.

data.headline:
Decompose the system
into a graph.
data.sub: From loop to enterprise systems  •  clarkhuang.github.io

scenes.text: Quick question. An agent hands you a plan. Ten steps, numbered one to ten. How many of those steps truly have to wait for the step before? [pause] All ten? About half? Or is it impossible to tell from the list? [pause] <emphasis>You can't tell.</emphasis> A numbered list records the order someone wrote things down. It doesn't say what needs what.

data.question:
A plan with ten numbered steps.
How many must wait for the step before?
options: You can’t tell from the list
data.why:
A list shows
writing order,
not what
needs what.

scenes.text: So here's the test. Take any two steps, and ask: what crosses between them? [pause] Think about cooking dinner. The sauce waits for the chopped onions. Something crosses, so that's a real dependency. Draw the arrow. [pause] The rice and the salad? Nothing crosses. So nobody waits for the rice before starting the salad. [pause] <slow>And then, is not a dependency.</slow>

data.label: THE TEST FOR ANY TWO STEPS
data.question: WHAT CROSSES?
data.caption: “And then” is not a dependency.

scenes.text: In one oh one, the unit was the loop. Plan, build, verify, until one piece of work is right. The graph sits one level up. It says which pieces exist, what each one needs, and which can run at the same time. [pause] And it doesn't replace the loop. Every node in the graph is <emphasis>still</emphasis> a loop of its own.

data.caption: Every node is still a loop.

scenes.text: Let's decompose a real system: the site you're on. Start with the parts. A.I. tips. Software engineering one oh one. Two oh one. And the book. Each part has its own folder, and its own pages. [pause] A new lesson in one needs nothing from the others. So work on one never waits on another.

data.label: CLARKHUANG.GITHUB.IO  ·  THE PARTS
data.caption:
No arrows
between them.
Nobody waits.

scenes.text: But they aren't floating free. All four are built by one generator, with one stylesheet. That shared piece is a node too, and every part depends on it. [pause] So the graph shows you where to be careful. Change one part, and one part moves. Change the shared node, and <emphasis>everything</emphasis> moves. Which is why a shared node needs one clear owner.

data.label: CLARKHUANG.GITHUB.IO  ·  THE PARTS, AND WHAT THEY SHARE
data.caption:
Change one part: one part moves.
Change the shared node: everything moves.

scenes.text: Now zoom into one node: a single video lesson. Here, the arrows are real. The narration clips need the script. The render needs those clips, because the length of the audio sets the timing. Captions need the timeline the render writes out. And the page needs all of it, before a pull request to staging, where only I merge to production. [pause] Every arrow carries something.

data.label: ONE LESSON OF THIS SITE  ·  WHAT EACH STEP NEEDS
data.caption: Every arrow carries something.

scenes.text: Script, narration, render. A strict chain. More agents won't make it shorter: the longest chain sets the minimum. [pause] But after the render, it forks. Captions need only the timeline. The sound level and the poster need only the video. Nothing crosses between those two. The build script happens to run them one after the other. The graph shows that's a choice, not a requirement.

data.label: ONE LESSON OF THIS SITE  ·  WHAT EACH STEP NEEDS
data.caption:
The longest chain sets the minimum.
The fork is where you get time back.

scenes.text: Why does this matter? Waiting. Picture three parts, with nothing crossing between them. Run as a numbered list, each one waits for the last. Run as a graph, they go side by side. Same work. Far less waiting.

data.label: TIME FROM START TO DONE  ·  AN ILLUSTRATION

bars.name: As a numbered list: each part waits for the last
As a graph: side by side

data.fine: THREE EQUAL PARTS, NOTHING CROSSING BETWEEN THEM

scenes.text: Now scale that up. Picture an enterprise system. Orders, billing, shipping, support. Far too big for one loop. [pause] It's the same picture. A few real arrows: billing needs the order, shipping needs the payment. A shared node everything leans on, like customer data. And parts that never touch, where teams and agents move without waiting. [pause] Miss the shared node, and two of them collide at the end.

data.label: PICTURE AN ENTERPRISE SYSTEM  ·  THE SAME GRAPH, BIGGER
data.caption: A few real arrows. A shared node. Parts that never touch.

scenes.text: So, to recap. Drawing the graph is four moves. One. Name the parts, each with a boundary and an owner. Two. For every pair, ask what crosses, and what they share. Three. Draw only those arrows. And four. Give every part its own finish line, and its own check.

data.headline: Drawing the graph: four moves
items: Name the parts: a boundary and an owner for each
For every pair: what crosses? What do they share?
Give every part its own finish line and check

scenes.text: Which gives us rule three, for your agents. Before any job with more than one part, draw the graph. Name the parts. Draw an arrow only where something crosses from one part to another. Anything two parts share becomes its own node, with one owner. Parts with no arrow between them run at the same time. And every part gets its own loop: plan, build, verify.

lines.text: Before any job with more than one part,
draw the graph: name the parts,
and draw an arrow only where something crosses.
Anything shared becomes its own node, with one owner.
No arrow? Those parts run at the same time.
Every part gets its own loop: plan, build, verify.

data.foot: THE FULL RULE IS ON THE LESSON PAGE

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Take the last multi-step plan an agent gave you. At every, and then, ask what crosses. [pause] How many arrows survive?

data.headline:
Your turn. Your last multi-step plan.
At every “and then”: what crosses?
How many arrows survive?

scenes.text: Next time, those parts really do run at once, and we bring the work back together. See you in lesson four.
